record.title: A preprint reports measurable retention loss across multi-agent research handoffs
record.summary: A September 15 preprint models how multi-agent decomposition affects the findings that survive to a root agent. It derives a yield relationship under a stated retention model and reports measurements from 600 production deep-research traces and 16,082 tool-result handoffs. The empirical estimates are author-reported and tied to one research scaffold.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors derive that, under their retention model r(b)=Cb^-δ, a depth-k tree over N findings yields C^k N^(1-δ), and report that flat organization is optimal for yield under the model.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 600 production deep-research traces, the authors report δ=0.34 (95% CI 0.30–0.38); across 16,082 tool-result handoffs, they report C=0.571 (95% CI 0.527–0.615). They report that each additional tier costs roughly 45% of yield in that measured setting.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution of the released scripts/corpora or replication of the reported constants was performed.
The empirical constants come from one research-agent scaffold; stability across other agents, task classes and tool boundaries is unmeasured.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported retention losses generalize, adding agent tiers could materially reduce how much useful research reaches decision makers, changing the expected value of multi-agent decomposition. The evidence is one author-reported paper and one research scaffold, so the consequence is conditional.
limitations: All empirical findings are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
The main trace corpus uses one research-agent scaffold; transfer to other systems or tasks is not established.
The analytical conclusion depends on the paper’s retention model and assumptions; it does not establish that flat systems are generally superior on total task quality, cost or latency.
brief.summary: A September 15 preprint models how multi-agent decomposition affects the findings that survive to a root agent. It derives a yield relationship under a stated retention model and reports measurements from 600 production deep-research traces and 16,082 tool-result handoffs. The empirical estimates are author-reported and tied to one research scaffold.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report δ=0.34 (95% CI 0.30–0.38) from 600 production deep-research traces and C=0.571 (95% CI 0.527–0.615) across 16,082 tool-result hops; under their model, each added tier reduces yield.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and its method, reported measurements and limitations are publicly accessible. This activation did not reproduce the empirical measurements.
technical.mechanism: The paper models an agent handed b items as retaining each with probability r(b), composes this retention across a decomposition tree, and measures retention using production traces plus tool outputs with explicit item boundaries.
technical.regime: The empirical work covers the authors’ production deep-research traces and tool calls. The formal derivation applies under the paper’s stated retention assumptions.
technical.strongest_baseline: Flat processing is the comparison for yield under the stated retention model; empirical C is measured at tool-result handoffs with explicit item boundaries.

brief.title: A preprint reports measurable retention loss across multi-agent research handoffs
brief.why_it_matters: If the measured loss generalizes, adding agent tiers can reduce the information that reaches a final decision maker, even when parallel agents surface more sources. The paper identifies a tradeoff between smaller working contexts and end-to-end retention that system designers can measure.
